title: The Challenge: Teachers Are More Than Guides on the Side
author: Ben Zulauf
summary: Ben Zulauf uses his personal experience co-creating a progressive, inquiry-based math curriculum as a case study for understanding why 'teacher as guide on the side' pedagogy fails, particularly for students from low-income households. He describes a curriculum assembled around proficiency groups, productive struggle, and student-driven problem solving—and then presents the data: achievement gaps between low-income and non-low-income students increased under this approach, while low-income students were disproportionately harmed. His central argument, drawing on Daniel Willingham, Rosenshine's Principles, and cognitive load theory, is that students cannot productively struggle their way to understanding without adequate prior knowledge in long-term memory, and that explicit instruction is not an obstacle to understanding but the mechanism by which understanding becomes possible. The article serves as a personal confession, a data-based critique of Danielson Framework assumptions about learning, and an argument that teachers who position themselves as facilitators rather than instructors are often doing so in ways that harm exactly the students most dependent on school for their academic growth.
points: Student-centered, inquiry-based math instruction systematically widens achievement gaps: Zulauf's data shows low-income students were disproportionately harmed by a curriculum built around productive struggle and discovery, because they lacked the prior knowledge needed to struggle productively.

The Danielson Framework's claim that 'a teacher's role is not so much to teach as it is to arrange for learning' is pedagogically dangerous when taken literally: students who don't have adequate background knowledge in long-term memory cannot benefit from being arranged into productive struggle.

Cognitive load theory explains the failure: working memory is limited, and when students are processing new content without adequate prior knowledge, cognitive load overwhelms the capacity to think, making discovery learning an exercise in confusion rather than understanding.

Rosenshine's Principles point toward what actually works: small steps, multiple examples, frequent checks for understanding, guided practice before independent practice, and scaffolding that gradually releases—direct instruction, not facilitation.

The guide-on-the-side framing is not neutral pedagogy: it reflects a set of beliefs about how learning works that are empirically contestable, and the students most harmed by those beliefs are consistently the ones most dependent on school for academic progress.
quotes: My role in this lesson was not to teach. It was to go from group-to-group to facilitate conversation and problem solving. This is what I tried to do. This is what I thought would be great for a recorded lesson for a whole committee of teachers to see.

One could argue that a teacher's role is not so much to teach as it is to arrange for learning. That is, a teacher's essential responsibility is to prepare for learning activities such that students learn. This is what I tried to do.
Our scores turned out exactly how you might expect. First, the achievement gap increased between our students from low income households vs. those from non low income.

Students in less proficient groups were given easier problems to start to build confidence. When groups finished with one set of problems, they were to send someone to get the next set, with each set gradually increasing in complexity. A lesson with zero instruction all in the name of problem solving and productive struggle.

We can see that it impacted students from low-income households more, experiencing a 2.9% decrease in proficiency from fourth to fifth grade. The achievement gap also increased by 1.5%, increasing from a 7.3% gap in proficiency to 8.8%.
